clue.text: One certainly, hopes a persistent won't

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'One certainly, hopes a persistent won't' is cut short: a noun after 'persistent' (bore?) is missing, so the cryptic definition cannot be read as printed.
annotationWithheld.clue: One certainly, hopes a persistent won't

clue.text: It's certainly able to give a good blow

definitions.text: It's certainly able to give a good blow

parts.words: It's certainly able to give a good blow
parts.note: sounds like a boxer or a gale, but describes a sea creature that spouts air and spray through its blowhole

explanation.surface: Praise for someone with a powerful punch.
explanation.definitionFit: A grampus is a dolphin-like whale (Risso's dolphin or the orca), and whales famously blow through their spouts.

clue.text: I left late — making the front page

indicators.note: the letters of the three words are worked into something new, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who walked out late still got on the front page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' is the anagram signal: the letters of I LEFT LATE rearrange to form the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A title leaf is the page at the front of a book that carries its title.

clue.text: Errant answer to a question of sanity?

definitions.text: answer to a question of sanity?
definitions.meaning: asked whether you are sane, a madman might reply '...'

explanation.surface: A wandering reply when someone asks whether you are sane.
explanation.definitionFit: Errant means wandering, and a wanderer with no fixed home is a nomad; split as 'no mad' it answers 'Are you sane?'

clue.text: This is going swimmingly !

parts.note: the everyday idiom for 'going well' is read literally, as a word describing something that swims

explanation.surface: A cheerful remark that things are going very well.
explanation.definitionFit: Natant is a formal adjective meaning swimming or floating, from Latin natare, to swim.

clue.text: Hard work with four, or six, in the series.

indicators.note: the Roman numeral is placed inside the word for a series

parts.note: a string is a series, as in a string of wins
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Doing four or six of something in a row takes real effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or six' is a neat extra: putting VI (six) inside STRING after its I gives the same answer, so either numeral works.
explanation.definitionFit: Striving is making great efforts, which is hard work.

clue.text: Tear in ten — just to be funny ?

definitions.text: Tear in ten — just to be funny ?

indicators.note: the letters are played about with for fun, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone rips up a tenner purely as a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just to be funny' is the anagram signal: TEAR IN TEN rearranges into the answer, and the whole clue also says what a prankster does to amuse.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain is to amuse, which is what a stunt done just to be funny aims at.

clue.text: Very lofty, this maiden.

parts.note: suggests a haughty young woman, but means a maiden who sits high in the heavens as a star sign

explanation.surface: A remark about a stuck-up young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgo, the Virgin, is a constellation and zodiac sign, so this maiden is literally high in the sky.

clue.text: They might undermine one's position.

parts.note: sounds like office rivals, but describes soldiers who dig tunnels and mines under enemy works

explanation.surface: A warning about colleagues who might weaken your standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Sappers are military engineers who dig saps and mines beneath fortifications.

clue.text: Essay produced by 5 dn.

definitions.meaning: an essay is an ... or trial, its older sense
5 down is STRIVING, and an effort is what striving produces

explanation.surface: A piece of writing written by sheer effort.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay is to try, so an essay is a try; striving at something produces a try at it.

clue.text: With which to catch a deserter

definitions.text: With which to catch a deserter

parts.words: With which to catch a deserter
parts.note: sounds like military police equipment, but a rat is slang for a deserter, so it is a device for catching rodents

explanation.surface: Asking what is used to capture a soldier gone absent without leave.
explanation.definitionFit: A rat is someone who deserts a cause, as rats leave a sinking ship, and a rattrap catches rats.

clue.text: To argue thus can be a soft way off.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'To argue thus can be a soft way off.': P (soft) + LEAD needs 'way' as LEAD and leaves 'off' with no job; the likely original ('soft pedal off', an anagram) is more than three letters from the print.
annotationWithheld.clue: To argue thus can be a soft way off.

clue.text: It was all the Raven had to say.

definitions.text: It was all the Raven had to say.

parts.words: It was all the Raven had to say
parts.note: points to Poe's poem The Raven, in which the bird repeats one word as its only reply

explanation.surface: A remark about a taciturn bird.
explanation.definitionFit: In Edgar Allan Poe's poem The Raven, the bird's sole utterance is its refrain 'Quoth the Raven'.

clue.text: Even the simplest enchantment may you to bad odour.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Even the simplest enchantment may you to bad odour.' lacks the verb after 'may' that would signal the hidden word in 'simplest enchantment'.
annotationWithheld.clue: Even the simplest enchantment may you to bad odour.

clue.text: "Mark!'where his carnage and his cease !" (Byron).

parts.words: Mark!'where his carnage and his cease
parts.note: a line from Byron's Childe Harold with one word missing between 'his' and 'cease', describing a warrior's victories

explanation.surface: A quotation from Byron about a conqueror's bloodshed ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's line in Childe Harold reads 'where his carnage and his conquests cease', victories won by force being what the gap needs.

clue.text: Utterly disgraceful this!

parts.note: an exclamation of outrage that simply describes a word meaning notorious for wrongdoing

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in shock at a scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Infamous means having a shameful reputation, thoroughly disgraceful.

clue.text: Carry on, not being knocked up.

definitions.text: Carry on, not being knocked up.

parts.words: Carry on, not being knocked up
parts.note: knocked up is British for woken by a knock at the door, so this means continuing to sleep because nobody wakes you

explanation.surface: Advice to keep going without being exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'knock up' traditionally means to wake someone by knocking, as a knocker-up did for workers before alarm clocks.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversleep is to go on sleeping past the time for rising, as happens when nobody calls you.

clue.text: Ride on me anyhow, it's bully

indicators.note: anyhow means in a careless, disordered way, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone invites another to ride roughshod over them, calling it bullying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' is the anagram signal: RIDE ON ME rearranges into the answer, and 'bully' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To domineer is to rule over others arrogantly, which is to bully them.

clue.text: Two directions for a drive?

parts.note: sounds like road directions, but in cricket a batsman's drive goes either to the off side or the on side

explanation.surface: A question about routes for a car journey.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the off side and on (leg) side are the two halves of the field, and a drive can be an off-drive or an on-drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-and-on means intermittently; it also names the two cricket sides a drive can be hit to.

clue.text: To do so may entail a call for a new suit.

definitions.text: To do so may entail a call for a new suit.

parts.words: To do so may entail a call for a new suit
parts.note: sounds like bidding in card games, where a new suit is called, but means a child getting too big for clothes

explanation.surface: A remark about switching suits in a game of bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: To outgrow something is to become too big for it, so clothes no longer fit and new ones are needed.

clue.text: Speculate perhaps-but without

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Speculate perhaps-but without (6)' is cut short after 'without': the second half (IN VEST, but without a jacket?) is missing.

clue.text: Expert on dates?

parts.note: sounds like a historian or a fruit grower, but means someone who often keeps romantic appointments

explanation.surface: A question about a historian who knows chronology.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is a lovers' secret meeting, a date, so one who makes trysts is practised at dates.

clue.text: The right bench to determine an issue.

definitions.meaning: a high-backed wooden seat with arms, the correct name for one kind of bench
to resolve a question or dispute

explanation.surface: Choosing the proper court bench to decide a case.
explanation.definitionFit: A settle is a long wooden bench with a high back; to settle a matter is to decide it.

clue.text: Not what one would expect to turn sour.

definitions.text: Not what one would expect to turn sour.

parts.words: Not what one would expect to turn sour
parts.note: sounds like milk or wine going off, but points to a gemstone with a sharp start and an unexpected sound

explanation.surface: Surprise that something good has gone bad.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer's opening, 'turq', echoes 'turn', and a precious blue stone is the last thing one expects to go sour.
explanation.definitionFit: Turquoise is a blue-green gemstone, not something that curdles, though its spelling starts like 'turn' and its sound like 'quoi'.

clue.text: To is worth ambition, though in hell" (Milton).

definitions.text: To is worth ambition, though in hell" (Milton).

parts.words: To is worth ambition, though in hell
parts.note: Satan's line from Milton's Paradise Lost with its second word missing, about ruling rather than serving

explanation.surface: A quotation from Milton about ambition even in hell.
explanation.definitionFit: In Paradise Lost, Satan says 'To reign is worth ambition though in Hell: Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heav'n.'

clue.text: To boggle like this — it's nonsensical.

parts.note: to boggle is to start back in fright, as a horse shies

explanation.surface: Being alarmed this way is just silly.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosh is nonsense, so toshy describes something rubbishy or nonsensical.

clue.text: Cast that meets with success.

definitions.meaning: to cast is to fling or hurl
in wrestling or judo, a move that brings the opponent down

explanation.surface: Describing a casting director's winning choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Throw means cast or hurl, and in wrestling a throw is the move that floors the opponent and scores.

clue.text: Second edition?

parts.note: a book printed again, put out a further time

explanation.surface: A question about a book's later printing.
explanation.definitionFit: To reissue is to publish again, so a second edition is a fresh issue.

clue.text: Old dame coming back about chaps' distress.

indicators.note: the reversed word goes round the word for chaps
the old woman's word is read in return, backwards

parts.note: a trot is an old word for an old woman
chaps are men

explanation.surface: An old woman returns, worried about some men's misery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming back' turns TROT into TORT, and 'about' puts it round MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Torment is severe suffering or anguish, a strong form of distress.

clue.text: One of two, usually, to clear the way one.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'One of two, usually, to clear the way one. (10,5)' is cut short: a word after 'way one' (sees?) is missing, so the cryptic definition does not read.
annotationWithheld.clue: One of two, usually, to clear the way one.
